opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a pretty speculative project, and I'd want to be upfront about that. The basic hope is this: when we look at a neural network and see it behave well on the training distribution, we'd like to understand *why*. Not a full proof, because proofs about these systems are basically hopeless, but something like the informal arguments mathematicians and physicists use all the time. "These two quantities are probably uncorrelated, so the expectation factors." "This term is small, so we can drop it." Those arguments are incredibly useful in practice, and we don't have a formal account of what makes them valid or how to combine them.

If we could formalize that, you could imagine a few big payoffs for alignment. One is detecting when a model's behavior on some new input is happening for a *different reason* than on training. That's the mechanistic anomaly detection idea. If the model normally says "the diamond is in the vault" because the diamond is in the vault, and on some new input it says it because the camera was tampered with, you'd like to flag that even if you can't tell the difference yourself. Another is estimating the probability of rare catastrophic behaviors that you'd never see by sampling.

How promising is it? I'd say we've made real progress in the sense that problems that looked confused a few years ago now look like crisp, if hard, technical questions. And I haven't seen anything that convinces me it's impossible. But there's a big gap between "no obvious obstruction" and "this will work." There's a real chance we hit a wall, either because there's no satisfying formalism or because it can't be made efficient enough for real models.

So my overall view is that it's a long shot, but a long shot with a large payoff, and one where nobody else is likely to do the work if we don't. A meaningful probability of success on something that could substantially change how we verify these systems seems worth a lot of effort, even if the most likely outcome is that we learn something partial and useful rather than getting the full thing.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say it's a long shot, but it's a long shot that I think is worth taking, and I'd put the probability that it works out in the sense I care about somewhere in the range of 10 to 20 percent. That's higher than I'd give most research directions in alignment, which is part of why I'm spending time on it.

The basic picture is that when you try to argue about what a neural network does, you very quickly run into cases where you can't give a proof. You'd like to say "this model never does X," and the honest answer is that the best you can do is something like a heuristic argument: here's why, if you treat these activations as roughly independent, or assume this part of the computation behaves like it did on the training distribution, the bad thing doesn't happen. Mathematicians do this all the time. They'll say the primes behave like random numbers in such and such a sense, and then derive a conjecture, and they'll be right surprisingly often. But there's no formal account of what makes one of those arguments good and another one bad, or of when you should update your beliefs and how much.

What we're trying to do is give a formal notion of what counts as a heuristic argument, and then a notion of what it means for an argument to be defeated by a better argument, so that you can actually run a process like "search for the best available argument that the model is safe, and search for counterarguments, and see what survives." If that worked, it would give you something much stronger than interpretability as it's currently practiced, because you'd have a principled account of why the explanation you found is the explanation, rather than just a story that happened to fit.

Where I'd temper the optimism is that we've been at this for a couple of years now and the core problem is still open. We have a bunch of partial results, like being able to say something sensible about the probabilities of certain structured events, and a lot of examples where we know what the right answer should be and our candidate definitions give the wrong answer. That's the normal state of a math research program, so I don't read too much into it, but I also wouldn't want to oversell where we are. The failure mode I worry about most is that there turns out to be no single clean notion, that "good heuristic argument" is just a messy pile of practices mathematicians have accumulated, and formalizing it is like formalizing good taste. If that's the case we'll have spent a few years and gotten some interesting but not load-bearing results.

The other thing I'd say is that even in the world where the formalization fails, I think the exercise is productive, because it forces you to be very precise about what it would mean to explain a model's behavior, and that precision tends to pay off in how you think about mechanistic interpretability and anomaly detection. So I think of it as a bet with a decent chance of a big payoff and a pretty good floor.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a long shot, but one that seems worth working on. The aspiration is to give a formal account of the kinds of arguments we use when we don’t have a proof—when we say, “This would be a surprising coincidence,” or “These two things should be roughly independent.” Those arguments do a huge amount of work in our understanding of the world, but we don’t have a very satisfying account of what makes them good arguments.

The hope is that you could make that reasoning precise enough to examine the assumptions and understand how the conclusion depends on them. For AI, that could help us reason about the behavior of a system even when a conventional proof would be out of reach.

The hard part is that you can write down rules that seem reasonable in individual examples, but then combining them can produce nonsense. You need an account of when you’re counting the same evidence twice, or when an apparent coincidence actually has an explanation you’ve overlooked.

So I’m more optimistic that there’s an interesting intellectual problem here than that solving it will give us a practical tool for AI alignment on the timeline we need. I’d like to get to the point where we can handle simple examples convincingly. That would give us a much better basis for judging how far the approach can go.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty speculative project. The hope is to give a mathematical account of what it means to have a good informal argument—an argument that falls short of a proof, but nevertheless gives you a reason to believe something.

A lot of our reasoning about complicated systems has that character. You can’t enumerate everything that might happen, so you make approximations, identify the considerations that seem important, and argue that the things you’re leaving out probably don’t change the conclusion. We don’t have a very satisfying formal account of when that works.

If you could develop one, it might help us understand how to get reliable judgments out of AI systems, including judgments about other AI systems. But there’s a large gap between producing a definition that captures some interesting examples and producing something useful for alignment. I’m interested in the project because it seems like it could clarify something fundamental, rather than because I’m confident it will lead to a practical solution.
